summary: Internal SE/AE enablement focused on sharpening positioning vs major competitors, practicing demo flows for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments, and aligning on next steps to produce battlecards and demo clips. Discussed common objections (latency, cost, security) and recommended phrasing and demo artifacts.
transcript:
[00:00] Avery: All right everyone, good morning — thanks for joining the enablement sesh. We'll run about 60 minutes. Quick intro round — who we have?
[00:10] Michael: Michael Lee here, sales enablement. Priya on my side will chime in as the AE manager.
[00:15] Priya: Hi yep, Priya. Thanks — excited to run through messaging.
[00:18] Jordan: Jordan Patel, SE — I'll drive the demo practice bits.
[00:22] Samira: Samira Ortiz, product marketing, I'll share the updated decks and the battlecard draft.
[00:28] Avery: Cool. Goal for today: get crisp on the 30-second pitch, handle the top three competitor objections, and run two quick demo role-plays: hosted API and dedicated/private scenario.
[00:38] Jordan: I'll start with the demo script I used last week — apologies in advance if it's rough, still working the timing.
[00:46] Samira: Quick note — I uploaded the latest battlecard to the enablement folder. Link in chat. It's called "battlecard_v3" but that might be a little off with examples.
[00:55] Avery: Perfect. Let's start with messaging. Samira, want to give the 30-second elevator?
[01:02] Samira: Yeah, trying: "Redwood Inference is a production‑first inference platform that gives teams predictable latency and unit economics across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — so you don't have to choose between cost and reliability."
[01:18] Priya: I like it. Can we tighten the bit about economics — customers often push back like "show me numbers".
[01:24] Samira: Good point, how about adding "with tooling to tune batching, caching and quantization to reduce per‑token cost by up to X%" — I left X as a placeholder so we don't overcommit.
[01:36] Michael: Be careful with percentages in the pitch unless we can back it up with a benchmark. Use 'meaningful' or 'material' unless you want to cite the benchmark.
[01:45] Jordan: For SEs, we should say: "we provide predictable throughput and fallbacks — so if a region's capacity is constrained, requests are automatically routed to compatible variants" — that's a good differentiator versus raw GPU infra.
[01:57] Avery: Good. Competitor framing — customers ask about OpenAI; how do we position?
[02:04] Samira: For OpenAI, emphasize the unified runtime and model catalog — we offer both cost controls and private deployment options. So phrasing: "OpenAI is great for rapid prototyping, but Redwood gives you predictable unit economics and private deployment paths for regulated workloads."
[02:18] Priya: And vs Anthropic?
[02:21] Jordan: Anthropic has model safety positioning — call out Redwood's quality monitoring and rollback ties to prompt sets/evals. Say: "we have quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets so you can detect drift or regressions during rollouts."
[02:34] Samira: Also add Hugging Face — customers like their model access but lack the operational runtime. So we say: "Hugging Face is great for model diversity; Redwood is the operational runtime that makes those models practical in production."
[02:47] Avery: Nice. Okay, let's practice the 30-second pitch round‑robin. Jordan go first and then Priya.
[02:55] Jordan: "Redwood Inference helps engineering teams ship LLM features with consistent performance across hosted, dedicated and private deployments. We combine a GPU‑optimized serving runtime, smart routing, and caching so you get predictable latency and lower per‑token costs — plus tooling for rollouts and observability."
[03:18] Priya: "Redwood is production-first — it gives you the SLAs, VPC/private options and cost controls you'd expect for enterprise workloads. If you're scaling from POC to production, Redwood reduces variability so product teams don't get surprised by latency or cost spikes."
[03:36] Michael: "One‑liner for execs — Redwood gets you predictable inference economics, operational controls and enterprise security so teams can focus on product not ops."
[03:49] Avery: Great. Move to demo practice. Jordan, run the hosted API happy path first — show streaming and a function call example. We'll time you.
[03:58] Jordan: Sure, launching demo... screen share — okay, showing terminal and the quick SDK snippet. So the first call is a streaming chat — you'll see token-by-token output.
[04:12] Jordan: (typing) I'll call the model, show streaming, then trigger a tool call to our imaginary FAQ service. You can see the stream arrive in under 200ms for the first bytes — note: lab conditions, your mileage may vary.
[04:28] Priya: Couple notes for the pitch: call out that streaming reduces perceived latency, and explain how prefix caching avoids re‑tokenizing common prompts.
[04:37] Jordan: Right, I'll say: "we leverage prefix/KV caching and continuous batching to reduce repeated compute on common prefixes."
[04:44] Samira: Watch the jargon — some AEs shorten to 'KV cache' but in docs it's 'KV cache / prefix caching'. Either's fine but be consistent.
[04:53] Jordan: Noted. Now demo the fallback — I'll show a canary rollout where we route to a cheaper quantized variant when demand spikes.
[05:04] Jordan: (narrating) Here's the routing policy in the console — latency target 200ms, fallback to quantized-gpt-2q variant, and a canary of 5%.
[05:15] Avery: Good to point out this is where you handle the latency vs cost objection — demonstrate concrete tradeoffs.
[05:21] Priya: Customers will ask: "how does quantization affect quality?" Have a one-liner: "we recommend quant profiles per workload and rollouts with evals to compare quality metrics — and we monitor for regressions tied to prompt sets."
[05:35] Jordan: I'll show the eval dashboard — here's a baseline vs quantized profile with example prompt set. You can see small delta on some tasks, big improvements on token cost.
[05:48] Samira: Add that the platform recommends quantization profiles based on historical token distributions — it's 'Redwood Optimize' tooling.
[05:56] Jordan: Small typo in my slide — said 'Optimize' as 'Optimise' — will fix.
[06:01] Michael: Question: what about private deployments? Can you demo the differences quickly?
[06:07] Jordan: Sure. Switching to the private control plane mock. Here you can see the VPC options and KMS integrations. For private/on‑prem we highlight SSO, RBAC, and audit logs.
[06:19] Jordan: (stumbles) the demo VM is a little slow today, apologies — but you can click through the 'networking' tab — VPC peering, route tables, and KMS/HSM toggles.
[06:29] Priya: Re: compliance — customers will want SOC2 and ISO certs. We should have a short canned answer: "We are SOC 2 Type II and pursuing ISO 27001; we also provide audit logs and KMS integrations for enterprise."
[06:41] Samira: Also have a doc link ready for SSO/SAML and per‑token data retention policies — send that after calls.
[06:48] Avery: We'll add that to the post-call kit.
[06:52] Jordan: Next I want to practice an objection: "We can't send PII to hosted providers."
[06:59] Priya: Response: "We support Private deployments with customer-managed VPC and optional on‑prem package; plus, RBAC, KMS, and audit logs ensure you stay compliant."
[07:10] Avery: If they need proof of controls, offer to run a short security review and share the SOC2 report — that's a standard step.
[07:17] Michael: Add that we can do a benchmark run in their environment or ours for latency and cost comparison.
[07:23] Jordan: Role-play time — I'll be AE, Priya be customer. Priya, throw one of the top objections.
[07:30] Priya: "Your cost sounds lower but how do I know it's not just smoke and mirrors?"
[07:35] Jordan: "Great question — we provide token-level cost breakdowns in the console and transparent post‑hoc billing reports; we can also run a short benchmark using your prompts to show real unit economics and latency numbers."
[07:48] Priya: "What if we have regional data residency needs?"
[07:51] Jordan: "We support region pinning and private control plane options — we can deploy in EU regions and enable data residency controls and log retention to meet regulatory requirements."
[08:03] Samira: Note for the battlecard — include the quick scripts to run a benchmark and a sample output so AEs can send concrete numbers.
[08:12] Avery: We're at the 30-minute mark. Let's do a shorter run: Jordan, do the 3-minute hosted flow and then the 3-minute private flow — focus on two demo hooks each.
[08:22] Jordan: (runs faster) Hosted: streaming + function calling + prefix cache highlight. Private: VPC/KMS + RBAC + audit logs.
[08:40] Jordan: Minor hiccup on tool call in hosted demo — sometimes dev envs drop websockets, mention fallbacks.
[08:48] Priya: Good callout — explain retry semantics and automatic fallback to polling if streaming is interrupted.
[08:56] Michael: On competitive rebuttals: when customers say "OpenAI is faster", we say: "OpenAI can be quick for starters; Redwood gives you consistent production latency and controls to keep costs predictable at scale."
[09:09] Samira: Also craft a line vs NVIDIA inference services — they sell hardware and infra; our message is we provide the orchestration, kernel selection and runtime that makes deploying models easier without hiring a big infra team.
[09:23] Jordan: There's also the edge case of customers that want GPU SKUs — we can map capacity to specific hardware in Dedicated and offer predictable throughput SLAs.
[09:33] Priya: Another practical ask — prospects ask for a short 2‑page 'what to expect' before POC. Samira can we create that?
[09:40] Samira: Yep, it's on my list — will include timeline, checkpoints, security docs and expected outputs.
[09:46] Avery: Okay, final recap and concrete next steps. Michael?
[09:50] Michael: We'll produce the battlecard v3 with competitor lines and sample benchmark scripts. We'll pack the post-call kit: SOC2 link, SSO guide, demo clips.
[09:59] Priya: We'll run role-play with EMEA reps next week.
[10:03] Avery: Thanks team. Quick action item recap: Samira finalize messaging deck; Jordan record demo clips; Avery share pricing examples; Michael book role-play.
[10:14] Jordan: One last note — watch for transcription quirks, sometimes 'KV cache' shows up as 'K V cash' in the transcript.
[10:20] Avery: Haha, yes. All right, meeting adjourned. Thanks everyone.

Notes: transcription contains typical ASR artifacts (names sometimes garbled). Links referenced: battlecard_v3 (internal drive), SOC2_report_link (internal), demo_clips folder.
